title: A timetable without clashes
summary: Clashes come from filling a whole sheet at once. Fill one period at a time, with a check on the teacher, and they stop.

sections.heading: Why timetables break
paragraphs: A timetable drawn on paper looks finished the day it is pinned up. The trouble shows on Monday: one teacher is expected in two rooms in the third period, and a section has a free slot nobody noticed.

These are not careless mistakes. A school with twenty sections and eight periods a day has well over a hundred and fifty slots to fill each day, and no one can hold every teacher’s week in their head while filling them.

sections.heading: Fix the bell schedule first
paragraphs: Before placing a single subject, agree when each period starts and ends, and where the breaks fall. Every section then shares the same grid, and "fourth period" means the same forty minutes to everyone.
Change the bell schedule in one place when winter timings begin, and every timetable follows.

sections.heading: Fill a slot, not a sheet
paragraphs: Build the timetable one cell at a time: pick the section, the day and the period, then choose the subject and the teacher. It is slower than copying last year’s sheet and far faster than untangling it in the second week.
In Sanchalix the grid refuses a teacher who is already teaching another section in that period. The clash is caught while you are still looking at the cell, not after the sheet has gone out.

sections.heading: Start with the teachers you have least of
paragraphs: Place the scarce ones first: the one physics teacher shared by four senior sections, the part-time music teacher who comes on two days. Subjects with several teachers will fit around them. Doing it the other way round leaves the scarce teacher with slots that do not exist.

sections.heading: Give every teacher their own day
paragraphs: A section’s timetable answers "what does 8-B have now?". A teacher needs the other view: where am I this period, and where next. Showing each teacher their own day on their home screen ends the walk to the staff room notice board.

sections.heading: Expect it to change
paragraphs: Teachers go on leave, a section is split, a lab is closed for a week. A timetable that can be changed one cell at a time, with the clash check still on, absorbs these without a new sheet being typed and photocopied.

title: Fee collection without the queue at the counter
summary: Most of the waiting at a fee counter is the office looking things up. Here is how to take that time out.

sections.heading: Where the time goes
paragraphs: Watch a fee counter on the tenth of the month and time one parent from "good morning" to the receipt in their hand. The payment itself takes seconds. The minutes go to finding the child in a register, working out which installment is due, checking whether last term was cleared and then writing a receipt by hand.
None of that is the cashier being slow. It is the cashier doing a lookup that the school already did once, when it set the fees for the year.

sections.heading: Decide the year once
paragraphs: Set each class’s fees and installments before the year starts, and have the principal approve them. From then on every student has their installments billed with a due date, and nobody at the counter is deciding what a family owes.
In Sanchalix this is a fee structure: what a class pays, split into installments by percentage. Approval issues the invoices for every student in those classes in one step.

sections.heading: Make the counter a search box
paragraphs: The cashier should type a name or an admission number and see that child’s open dues, oldest first. They tick what is being paid, choose cash, UPI, card or cheque, and the receipt prints with its number.
Part payments are normal, not an exception. A family that pays half today should leave with a receipt for half and a clear balance, not a note in the margin.

sections.heading: Let reminders do the chasing
paragraphs: A dues list sorted by how late each payment is tells the office who to call first. A reminder sent to every parent with an overdue installment, in one action, replaces a week of phone calls with an afternoon of the difficult ones.

sections.heading: What to keep on paper
paragraphs: The printed receipt, signed if your school signs them. Parents value it and auditors ask for it. What you can stop keeping is the second handwritten copy and the ledger that exists only so someone can add it up.

title: Attendance that parents can trust
summary: A register is only useful if it is taken the same way every day and the family hears about an absence the same morning.

sections.heading: Start from present
paragraphs: On an ordinary day almost everyone is in class. A register that starts every child as present and asks the teacher to change only the exceptions takes a minute, and a minute is short enough that it gets done before the first period, every day.

sections.heading: One person owns each section
paragraphs: When any teacher can mark any class, nobody is sure who did. Give each section a class teacher who takes its daily attendance, and let subject teachers take period attendance only where the school needs it, usually the senior classes.

sections.heading: Tell the family the same morning
paragraphs: An absence message that arrives in the evening is a record. One that arrives by mid-morning is useful: the parent who sent their child to school knows straight away that something is wrong.
Send it only after the register is submitted, and only for absences. Parents stop reading a school that messages them about everything.

sections.heading: Corrections are fine, silent ones are not
paragraphs: Teachers make mistakes and children arrive late. Allow the day’s register to be changed on the day, and after that let a senior person correct it with a reason that is kept. A register that can never change is wrong for ever; one that changes without a trace is not a register.

sections.heading: Holidays should not count
paragraphs: Mark holidays and non-working days once, in the school calendar, and attendance percentages take care of themselves. The 75 percent question at the end of the year should be an answer you read off, not a calculation.

title: Admissions: from the first enquiry to the first day
summary: Admissions go wrong in the gaps between stages. Naming the stages, and what moves a family from one to the next, closes most of them.

sections.heading: Write down every enquiry
paragraphs: The family that phoned in January and never heard back is the seat you could not fill in April. Record every enquiry the day it comes in, with the class sought and a phone number, even if nothing else is known yet.

sections.heading: Name the stages
paragraphs: Enquiry, applied, documents pending, assessment, offered, admitted. The names matter less than everyone using the same ones, so that "where is this child’s application?" has one answer.
Each move should leave a line of history: who moved it, when, and a note if there was a reason. That history is what you read when a parent says they were told something different.

sections.heading: Ask for documents early, check them once
paragraphs: Decide which documents the school must see before a child is admitted, usually a birth certificate and a photograph, and collect them while the application is still open. Checking each one once, and recording that it was checked, is better than asking the family again in June.

sections.heading: Make admitting a single step
paragraphs: The moment a seat is confirmed, the child needs a student record, an admission number, a class and section, and their parents on file. Doing these as four jobs on four days is how a child ends up in class without a roll number.
In Sanchalix, admitting an applicant creates all of it together, or none of it, and carries the checked documents across to the student.

sections.heading: Count what you turned away
paragraphs: At the end of the season, look at how many enquiries reached each stage. If most families drop out between enquiry and application, the form is the problem. If they drop out after the offer, it is usually fees or timing.

title: Report cards without the last-week rush
summary: The rush before results day is marks arriving late and being typed twice. Both can be designed out.

sections.heading: Agree the papers before the exam
paragraphs: For each exam, list every class’s papers with the date and the maximum marks before the first one is written. A teacher who knows that Class 8 Science is out of 80 will not hand in marks out of 100.

sections.heading: Marks are entered once, by the teacher
paragraphs: The person who marked the paper should be the person who enters the marks, in one place. Every copy from a mark sheet into a register and then into a report card is a chance to turn 67 into 76.
Entry should refuse a mark above the maximum and make "absent" a choice, not a zero.

sections.heading: Lock, then publish
paragraphs: Give the principal a clear step between "marks are in" and "families can see them". Locking a paper says the marks are final; unlocking one should need a reason that is kept. Publish only when every paper is locked.

sections.heading: Generate, then add what only a teacher knows
paragraphs: Totals, percentages and grades are arithmetic and should be generated. The class teacher’s time is better spent on the one thing that cannot be: a remark that sounds like it was written about this child.

sections.heading: Publish to families on one day
paragraphs: When report cards go out for a whole section at once, every family sees them at the same time and the office is not asked forty times whether results are ready.

title: Moving a school off paper registers, one term at a time
summary: Schools that change everything in a week go back to paper in a month. An order that works, and what to leave for later.

sections.heading: Start with the list of students
paragraphs: Everything else hangs off it. Get every current student in with their class, section, roll number and one parent’s phone number. Import them from the spreadsheet you already have, check it with a trial run first, and fix the rows that fail.
Do not wait for perfect data. A correct name, class and phone number is enough to start; the rest can be filled in as families come to the office.

sections.heading: Then attendance
paragraphs: It is daily, it is quick, and teachers see the benefit within a week. Run it alongside the paper register for a fortnight if that makes people comfortable, then stop the paper one.

sections.heading: Then fees
paragraphs: Fees are where mistakes cost money, so move them at a boundary: the start of a term or a year. Set the structures, have them approved, and collect the new term through the system from day one. Finish the old term in the old ledger; do not try to type in history.

sections.heading: Exams and report cards last
paragraphs: They happen a few times a year, so there is no hurry, and by then the students, classes and teachers are already in place. Try one unit test before you trust it with the half-yearly.

sections.heading: Give everyone their own sign-in
paragraphs: A shared office password means nobody knows who changed what. Each person signs in as themselves, with the role that matches their job, and the record of who did what keeps itself.

sections.heading: What changes for the principal
paragraphs: The questions you used to ask the office, you can now look up: who is absent today, what was collected this week, which sections have not submitted attendance, which fee structures are waiting for you. That is the point of the whole exercise.

title: Your first week with Sanchalix
summary: You do not need to switch everything on at once. A short order for the first week keeps the office calm and the data clean.

sections.heading: Start with people, not features
paragraphs: The first week goes wrong when a school tries to start every module on Monday. Staff learn five new screens at once, mistakes pile up, and by Friday the old register is back on the desk.
Start with the records everything else depends on: classes and sections, then staff, then students. A timetable, an invoice or a report card is only as good as the people attached to it.

sections.heading: Days one and two: set up the year
paragraphs: Create the academic year, the classes and their sections, and the subjects each class studies. Do this once, with the principal in the room, so the decisions are made by the person who owns them.
Then add staff and give each teacher the sections they teach. A teacher who signs in and sees only their own classes understands the system in a minute.

sections.heading: Days three and four: bring the students in
paragraphs: Import students from your existing spreadsheet rather than typing them again. Check a handful of records by hand, especially phone numbers, because those decide whether a parent ever receives a message.
Fix errors in the file and import again instead of patching records one by one. It is faster, and the next import will be cleaner.

sections.heading: Day five: take attendance for real
paragraphs: End the week by taking attendance in Sanchalix for one full day, alongside the paper register. Compare the two on Monday.
This is the habit that makes everything else useful. Once attendance is daily, parents see it, the office stops chasing absentees, and the dashboard starts showing something true.

sections.heading: What can wait
paragraphs: Fees, exams and the timetable are better started in the second or third week, once the team is comfortable. Nothing is lost by waiting, and each module goes in cleaner on top of records people already trust.

title: Fee reminders that parents actually read
summary: A reminder that is late, vague or sent to everyone gets ignored. Send it early, say the amount, and send it only to those who owe.

sections.heading: Why most reminders fail
paragraphs: A message that says “fees are due” to the whole school teaches parents to ignore it. Half of them have already paid, and the rest cannot tell whether it is about them.
A reminder works when it is specific enough that the parent can act without calling the office.

sections.heading: Say who, how much and by when
paragraphs: Name the child, the installment, the amount and the last date. “Aarav’s second installment of ₹6,000 is due on 10 November” answers every question the parent would have asked.
Keep it to one message with one clear next step, such as paying at the counter or online.

sections.heading: Send it twice, not ten times
paragraphs: One reminder a few days before the due date and one the day after it passes is enough for most families. More than that reads as pressure and costs SMS credits.
Families who still have not paid after the second reminder are the ones worth a phone call, and now the list is short enough to call.

sections.heading: Never send it to people who have paid
paragraphs: Build the list from open dues, not from the class list. A parent who paid last week and is reminded anyway loses trust in every later message, including the ones that matter.

sections.heading: Be kind about part payments
paragraphs: Many families pay in parts. Show the remaining balance, not the original amount, so a parent who has paid half sees that the school noticed.

title: An exam schedule without clashes
summary: Exam week fails when two papers share a room or a student. Settle the rules first and the date sheet almost writes itself.

sections.heading: Start from the constraints
paragraphs: An exam schedule has three limits: a student cannot sit two papers at once, a room holds only so many, and an invigilator cannot be in two halls. Write these down before choosing a single date.
Most clashes come from choosing dates first and checking afterwards.

sections.heading: Give each class its own order
paragraphs: Place the heavier subjects early in the week and leave a day between the two hardest. Students prepare better, and the results show it.
Keep the same order across sections of a class so that nobody asks why one section had an easier week.

sections.heading: Assign invigilators last
paragraphs: Once rooms and papers are fixed, assign invigilators from teachers who are free in those periods, and avoid a teacher invigilating the subject they teach.
Spread the duty evenly. A teacher with four invigilations in two days is not marking well on the third.

sections.heading: Publish early and freeze it
paragraphs: Share the date sheet with parents and students at least two weeks ahead. After that, change it only for something serious, and tell everyone the same day.

title: Half-days, leave and attendance percentages
summary: A school’s attendance figure is only as fair as its rules. Decide how half-days and approved leave count before the term starts.

sections.heading: The number everyone asks about
paragraphs: Boards and schools set a minimum attendance percentage for exam eligibility, and parents ask about it more than almost any other figure. If two teachers count it differently, the result is an argument at the office door.
The fix is to agree the rules once and apply them the same way for every student.

sections.heading: Decide how a half-day counts
paragraphs: A student who arrives late or leaves at noon is neither fully present nor fully absent. Many schools count a half-day as half a day present, and the school’s own policy should say so in writing.
Whatever you choose, record the half-day as it happened. The percentage is then calculated, not guessed.

sections.heading: Treat approved leave separately
paragraphs: Illness with a note and a family function with prior notice are different from an unexplained absence. Record the reason when the leave is approved, so the register shows why a child was away.
Keep the reason visible to teachers and the office, but not wider than that. A child’s medical details are not for everyone.

sections.heading: Tell families before it matters
paragraphs: A parent who learns in March that attendance is at 68% cannot do anything about it. Send a gentle note when a child first drops under the limit, and again if it continues.
Early information changes the number. Late information only explains it.
